title: Connecting Stock Market to Labor Market During the AI Boom - San Francisco Fed
gist: Lansing and Nucera (SF Fed) show a model using r-star, g-star, u-star and macro uncertainty explains 89% of S&P 500 CAPE variance since 1961 and most of the AI-era run-up to 40.5 (fitted 35.8, ~12% rich). The noncyclical unemployment rate u-star is the key variable—without it fitted CAPE is 21.4 (47% below actual)—linking stock valuations to the labor market, though sustainability of AI-era valuations is not guaranteed.

insights.claim: As of Q3 2026 the S&P 500 cyclically adjusted price-earnings (CAPE) ratio stood at 40.5, higher than every prior technology-boom peak since the late 1800s except the 43.1 reached in Q1 2000.
insights.speaker: Kevin Lansing
insights.so_what: US equity valuations are within ~6% of the dot-com record, leaving little valuation cushion if AI fundamentals disappoint.
insights.quote: As of the third quarter of 2026, the CAPE ratio stood at 40.5.
insights.locator: The CAPE ratio and macroeconomic variables

insights.claim: Major stock price run-ups have historically coincided with 'new era' narratives around a new technology: railroads and electricity (early 1900s), autos and radio (late 1920s), semiconductors and TV (1950s-60s), the internet (late 1990s), social networks/cloud/EVs (peak late 2021), and now AI starting with ChatGPT's release in November 2022.
insights.speaker: Kevin Lansing
insights.so_what: Treat the AI run-up as the sixth instance of a recurring tech-narrative valuation cycle; history shows such peaks tend to be followed by de-rating.
insights.quote: Major stock price run-ups have generally coincided with the emergence of some new era narrative centered on the introduction of a new technology
insights.locator: The CAPE ratio and new eras

insights.claim: The AI boom shares the hallmarks of past technology booms: a 'new era' narrative, surging investment in affected sectors, and elevated CAPE valuations.
insights.speaker: Kevin Lansing
insights.so_what: Use narrative + capex surge + elevated CAPE as a checklist to recognize late-cycle tech-boom dynamics.
insights.locator: The artificial intelligence (AI) boom shares features

insights.claim: A regression of log CAPE on the neutral real rate (r-star), potential output growth (g-star), the noncyclical unemployment rate (u-star) and a macro uncertainty index explains 89% of CAPE variance from 1961 to Q3 2026, with all four variables statistically significant.
insights.speaker: Kevin Lansing
insights.so_what: Long-run equity valuation multiples are largely explainable by slow-moving macro fundamentals, so shifts in these variables are the key valuation drivers to monitor.
insights.quote: The in-sample fit is excellent, accounting for 89% of the variance in the CAPE ratio.
insights.locator: All four macroeconomic variables are statistically significant

insights.claim: Consistent with present-value theory, higher r-star, higher u-star and higher macro uncertainty all lower the CAPE ratio, while faster potential growth (g-star) raises it.
insights.speaker: Kevin Lansing
insights.so_what: A rise in neutral rates or uncertainty, or a slowdown in trend growth, is a fundamental headwind to equity multiples.
insights.locator: Consistent with theory, the estimated coefficients

insights.claim: A lower risk-free rate or less uncertainty reduces the discount applied to future cash flows, raising fundamental stock prices, while faster expected cash-flow growth also implies a higher price; r-star proxies the risk-free rate and g-star drives real cash-flow growth.
insights.speaker: Kevin Lansing
insights.so_what: Frames valuation as discount-rate vs growth: watch Fed r-star estimates and CBO potential growth as valuation inputs.
insights.locator: In theory, the fundamental stock price is the present value

insights.claim: Over the long sample the CAPE ratio trended down before 1980 and up thereafter, while u-star did the opposite (rising before 1980, declining after); r-star and g-star both trended down, with r-star's decline more pronounced.
insights.speaker: Kevin Lansing
insights.so_what: The secular post-1980 rerating aligns with falling structural unemployment and falling neutral rates; reversal of either would threaten multiples.
insights.locator: The CAPE ratio trends mostly downward before 1980

insights.claim: The noncyclical unemployment rate (u-star) is the single most important explanatory variable for the CAPE ratio: dropping it cuts the model's explained variance from 89% to 49%.
insights.speaker: Kevin Lansing
insights.so_what: Structural labor-market health is a first-order equity valuation signal; a rising u-star would be a major bearish valuation input.
insights.quote: Estimated without u-star, the model accounts for only 49% of the variance in the CAPE ratio.
insights.locator: All four macroeconomic variables are statistically significant

insights.claim: Stock and labor markets are linked because both are present-value calculations: investors value future cash flows from stocks and employers value future benefits from new hires, so a lower discount rate lifts stock prices and hiring, pushing down unemployment and, in the long run, u-star.
insights.speaker: Kevin Lansing
insights.so_what: Expect equity valuations and structural hiring strength to move together; deteriorating hiring could foreshadow multiple compression.
insights.quote: employers value the future benefits from hiring new workers in much the same way that investors value future cash flows from stocks

insights.claim: Improvements in job-matching efficiency may also connect the two markets by pairing workers and employers better, boosting worker productivity and the profitability of publicly traded firms.
insights.speaker: Kevin Lansing
insights.so_what: If AI improves job matching, it could support both lower structural unemployment and corporate earnings.
insights.locator: The two markets may also be linked through improvements in job-matching

insights.claim: In Q3 2026 the model including u-star yields a fitted CAPE of 35.8, 11.6% below the actual 40.5, implying the AI-era run-up is mostly explained by fundamentals.
insights.speaker: Kevin Lansing
insights.so_what: Under this model the US market is only modestly rich—roughly 12% above fundamental-implied valuation.
insights.quote: the model with u-star yields a fitted CAPE ratio of 35.8, which is 11.6% below the actual ratio of 40.5

insights.claim: Without u-star, the same macro model yields a fitted Q3 2026 CAPE of just 21.4, implying a 47.2% drop from the actual 40.5—showing that fundamental-value assessments are highly sensitive to model specification.
insights.speaker: Kevin Lansing
insights.so_what: The 'fair value' range for US equities spans roughly 12% to 47% downside depending on whether labor-market structure is credited; valuation conclusions are fragile.
insights.quote: assessments of fundamental stock market value can be highly sensitive to the details of the underlying model
insights.locator: The model with u-star fits the actual CAPE ratio quite well

insights.claim: Both model versions place fitted CAPE below the actual ratio during the late-1990s internet boom, indicating the market was overvalued then, and both predicted sharp CAPE drops in the high-uncertainty 2008-2009 financial crisis.
insights.speaker: Kevin Lansing
insights.so_what: Unlike 2000, today's CAPE is largely explained by the u-star model—a key distinction for anyone calling the AI boom a dot-com rerun.
insights.locator: Figure 3 plots the actual versus fitted

insights.claim: The model without u-star wrongly predicts an exceptionally large CAPE decline in early 2020 because it overweights uncertainty, yet the pandemic uncertainty spike hit valuations far less than the comparable 2008-2009 spike; the u-star model fits 2010-2026 well, including the transitory 2020 dip.
insights.speaker: Kevin Lansing
insights.so_what: Uncertainty spikes do not map uniformly into valuation drawdowns; context (e.g., labor-market structure) matters.
insights.locator: The model with u-star fits the actual CAPE ratio quite well from 2010

insights.claim: Greenwald, Lettau and Ludvigson (2025) find the decline in labor's share of US national income has been the most important driver of rising stock valuations since the late 1980s, as more income accrues to capital owners, with automation and eroding worker bargaining power as proposed causes.
insights.speaker: Kevin Lansing
insights.so_what: If AI accelerates automation and further shifts income to capital, it could structurally support higher multiples; a labor-share rebound would be a headwind.
insights.locator: The decline in labor's share of U.S. national income

insights.claim: Replacing u-star with the trend labor share in the CAPE model gives a negative, highly significant coefficient but explains only 71% of variance versus 89% for u-star, largely because u-star also captures the pre-1980 period when it rose while CAPE fell.
insights.speaker: Kevin Lansing
insights.so_what: u-star is the more robust single labor-market valuation indicator across regimes.
insights.locator: Figure 4 shows the U.S. labor share of income

insights.claim: Since 1980 the parallel declines in u-star and the labor share suggest both may be responding to common structural forces reshaping the labor market.
insights.speaker: Kevin Lansing
insights.so_what: Watch for AI-driven labor-market restructuring as a common driver of both structural unemployment and capital's income share.
insights.locator: After 1980, the downward trends observed in u-star

insights.claim: Even though a four-variable macro model explains most of the AI-linked CAPE run-up, its historical fit does not guarantee that a CAPE of 40.5 is sustainable, because the underlying relationships may change.
insights.speaker: Kevin Lansing
insights.so_what: Don't treat model-explained valuations as safe; regime change in macro relationships is the key tail risk.
insights.quote: the model’s ability to fit the historical data does not guarantee that the current CAPE ratio of 40.5 is sustainable

insights.claim: Previous technology-driven booms were accompanied by 'this time is different' narratives justifying high valuations, and it remains open whether AI enthusiasm will be validated by sustained fundamental improvements or prove another episode of overly optimistic expectations.
insights.speaker: Kevin Lansing
insights.so_what: Position for two-sided outcomes: AI must deliver sustained fundamental gains (e.g., lower u-star, higher growth) to justify current multiples.
insights.quote: Previous technology-driven booms were accompanied by “this time is different” narratives
